extracted.intended_audience: literate coffee-house readers and general public interested in news, morals, and periodical essays (early-18th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical essays commenting on the nature and value of news, the harms of anonymous defamatory writing (libel/satire), and what kinds of writing or reporting are valuable to readers. Offers prescriptive judgments about authorship, readership, and news content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anonymous publication only with caution (registration proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal: oblige every Person that writes a Book, or a Paper, to swear himself the Author of it, and enter down in a publick Register his Name and Place of Abode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This would suppress printed scandal (libels) which commonly appear under borrowed names or none; but it would also 'destroy Learning' by discouraging anonymous beneficent works and deterring authors from trying their work in the world. The page argues that very few works of genius are published initially with the author's name and that forced disclosure would root up 'Corn and Tares together.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamatory/satirical writing is scandalous and destructive
rubrics_metrics.description: Satyrical, scurrilous, or defamatory papers and pamphlets are scandalous to government and detestable to good men; they 'ruin the Honour of Families' and make the nation appear monstrous to outsiders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such writings are compared to murderers and assassins in moral gravity; they subvert truth and humanity, lower public discourse, and should be discouraged and punished. The essay cites historical/legal authorities (Cicero, twelve Tables, Roman law) to show libel was severely punished and urges magistrates to mark their displeasure to deter the practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers share culpability for consuming/dispersing libels
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who take pleasure in reading or dispersing a defamatory libel are morally blameworthy, possibly as guilty as the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting authorities (St. Gregory, Roman maxim), the essay argues the approver of a crime is like the adviser; therefore those who approve, read, or spread libels contribute to the harm and deserve condemnation or penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural writing rooted in observation is preferable to speculative froth
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing that is 'natural'—pleasing, easy, grounded in observation and useful judgment—is superior to scholastic speculation or frothy amusing conceits dressed in quaint language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tradesman-writer contrasts profitable observation and plain narrative with 'wits or philosophers' who favour invention/speculation. 'Natural' writing is defined as that which is pleasing and easy; avoiding mere novelty-for-novelty's-sake and ornamental conceits which suit only 'Boys or silly Women.'

rubrics_metrics.name: News should be substantial, informative, and enduring (prefer history/travel to ephemeral scraps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers' voracious appetite for novelty makes them relish everything 'that is Matter of Fact,' but the essay recommends turning that appetite toward History, Travels, and writings with perpetual fuel for curiosity rather than transient daily scraps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A victory or trivial item may entertain for a post or a day, but comprehensive historical narratives or travel accounts provide continued pleasure and improvement. The essay suggests that campaigns or histories can be read more efficiently than following daily suspense, thereby avoiding the 'eternal Thirst' of modern news-mongers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness criteria: novelty, matter-of-factness, freshness, and local relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Items that are new, matter-of-fact, and fresh (recent arrivals, local occurrences within the penny-post) satisfy public curiosity; novelty and immediacy are decisive for many readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed daily paper of local intelligence would exploit low carriage cost and daily receipt to supply 'fresh and fresh' news — from horse impoundments to local weddings — showing that novelty, proximity, and frequency make content desirable even if trivial. The essay also notes that many readers value novelty over importance ('Voracious Appetite, but no Taste').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid redundant, derivative reporting; provide distinct commentary or unique value
rubrics_metrics.description: The same piece of intelligence is often repeated 'in the same Words' across several writers; though text is supplied by one set, commentaries are by another, resulting in redundancy and little added value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay criticises multiplicity of copies and recommends either original reporting or meaningful, varied commentary rather than repeating identical tales or merely echoing foreign posts. Editors/writers should aim to add distinct reflections rather than reprinting the same intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of the reader's relation to news: relevance over exotic curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: All matters of fact are not equally relevant; an Englishman has more concern for his own nation's history than for the affairs of distant rivers or foreign courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and readers should prioritize news that has clear relevance or importance to their own lives and civic identity rather than indulging an indiscriminate taste for novelty from remote places.
